Keywords: low-temperature processing | magnetron sputtering | Ta-doped tin oxide | TCOs | transparent conductive oxides

The formation of the transparent conductive oxide  $ SnO_{2} $:Ta by reactive direct-current magnetron sputtering at a low temperature of  $ 225^{\circ}C $ was studied as a function of the oxygen flow rate using a pilot-scale setup. Beginning with a mixture of  $ \beta $-Sn and SnO as majority phases and minority fractions of  $ Sn_{3}O_{4} $ and  $ SnO_{2} $ at very low  $ O_{2} $ flows, up to the formation of phase-pure rutile-type  $ SnO_{2} $:Ta at higher flow rates, a systematic evolution of the phase structure is observed. The  $ SnO_{2} $:Ta (0.70 at.% Ta) film grown at optimized flow conditions exhibits a transmittance of >80% from 500 to 2500 nm and a specific resistivity of  $ 0.3\ \Omega cm $. While the transmittance is competitive, the resistivity is in the upper range of that reported for low-temperature-deposited  $ SnO_{2} $:Ta films in research lab studies. Based on X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, optical spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, we conclude that the small crystallite size, microstrain, and point defects caused by the low growth temperature might prevent charge carrier activation, even though the Ta dopant is incorporated as  $ Ta^{5+} $ in the rutile-type  $ SnO_{2} $ lattice.

Among the three classical transparent conductive oxides (TCOs) such as  $ In_{2}O_{3} $, ZnO, and  $ SnO_{2} $, the latter is distinguished by a high chemical, mechanical, and thermal stability [1-3]. The most abundantly used dopant for  $ SnO_{2} $ is fluorine [4-7].  $ SnO_{2}:F $ can be used as a transparent electrode in display technologies, as a low-emissivity glass coating to improve the energy efficiency of buildings by reducing the infrared heat transmission while still retaining the transparency for visible light, or as a spectrally selective coating for solar collectors [3, 8, 9]. Recently, the research focus for  $ SnO_{2} $-based TCOs has shifted to the investigation of tantalum-doped  $ SnO_{2} $ (TTO) thin films because of their superior electrical properties and higher thermal stability in vacuum and air [10-14]. This latter material property is especially critical as these films can find an application as a capacitor electrode in data storage devices, or as a solar-selective transmitter in concentrated solar power plants that require a heat resistance up to 800°C [15, 16]. Because this material demonstrates the potential to be used in a wide range of applications, the necessary tunability to meet the different technical specifications requires the use of scalable low-temperature deposition techniques.

To date, TTO thin films exhibiting the best transport properties were pulsed-laser deposited.  $ Sn_{0.95}Ta_{0.05}O_2 $ films epitaxially grown on rutile  $ TiO_2 $ (110) single-crystal substrates at  $ 800^\circ C $ showed a resistivity of  $ 1.1 \times 10^{-4} \Omega cm $, and  $ Sn_{0.997}Ta_{0.003}O_2 $ films grown at  $ 600^\circ C $ had the maximum charge carrier mobility for TTO with  $ 130 \, cm^2 $ ( $ Vs)^{-1} $ [11, 17].
